title: The Chelsea Hotel
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explore the Chelsea Hotel in New York City, from its 1884 construction as a Victorian Gothic housing co-op inspired by Charles Fourier, through its decades as a bohemian hotel and artist residence. They cover famous residents and guests (Thomas Wolfe, Dylan Thomas, Bob Dylan, Edie Sedgwick, Janis Joplin and Leonard Cohen, Patti Smith and Robert Mapplethorpe, Sid Vicious and the death of Nancy Spongen, Ethan Hawke), the Bard family's management under David and Stanley Bard, notable deaths and drug culture, and the post-2007 sale, staff firings, art removal and controversial renovation, followed by auctioned relics and listener mail about finger spelling.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

entities.name: Sad Eyed Lady of the Lowlands

segments.title: Opening banter and naming the Chelsea Hotel
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode as part of their New York series and discuss the hotel's official name (Hotel Chelsea vs. Chelsea Hotel) and a Marriott in the neighborhood. They note the hotel's renovation and its landmark status.

segments.title: Construction and early history as a housing co-op
segments.summary: The building opened in 1884 at West 23rd Street as the Chelsea Association Building, a twelve-story Victorian Gothic designed by Philip Hubert based on Charles Fourier's utopian ideas. It began as a housing co-op with shared ownership and reserved apartments for builders and artists.

segments.title: Artists, bohemian culture and early famous guests
segments.summary: After the co-op went bankrupt in 1905, the building became a hotel with long-term residents and weekly and monthly rates. Artists lived there, and early guests included Mark Twain, Sarah Bernhardt, and Titanic survivors in 1912. Thomas Wolfe lived there and died young; the Ashcan School artists were associated with it.

segments.title: Literary residents and Dylan Thomas
segments.summary: Edgar Lee Masters wrote a poem about the hotel and worried about its future. Dylan Thomas lived there and died in 1953, which added to its reputation for tragic figures. Jackson Pollock, Virgil Thomson and Larry Rivers were also longtime or notable residents.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Break before returning to the Bard family history.

segments.title: David and Stanley Bard's management
segments.summary: David Bard bought the hotel out of foreclosure in 1943 and kept the policy of accepting art in lieu of rent. His son Stanley Bard ran it for about forty years, with a famously tolerant approach, and residents were often vouched for by existing artists. Arthur Miller and a vacuum cleaner anecdote illustrate Stanley's style.

segments.title: Deaths at the hotel and the Bards' tolerance
segments.summary: Milos Forman asked Stanley whether anyone had died there; Stanley could recall only painter Al Fais Cole, who died in 1988 at 112. David Bard refused to evict a drummer, saying he liked people. Arthur Miller described the hotel as a house of infinite toleration.

segments.title: Sixties and seventies: Bob Dylan, Warhol and Edie Sedgwick
segments.summary: Bob Dylan stayed in room 211 and wrote parts of Blonde on Blonde, including Sad Eyed Lady of the Lowlands. Andy Warhol and Dylan reportedly competed over Edie Sedgwick, and Sedgwick later set her mattress on fire. Arthur C. Clarke and Warhol's Chelsea Girls were also linked to the hotel.

segments.title: Drugs, families and celebrity residents
segments.summary: Drug use was a major part of hotel life. Gaby Hoffman grew up there, and her mother Viva wrote an unpublished book about her. Leonard Cohen and Janis Joplin had a relationship there; Cohen wrote Chelsea Hotel No. 2. Patti Smith and Robert Mapplethorpe lived there while broke, and Mapplethorpe's work drew controversy and Jesse Helms opposed NEA funding.

segments.title: Al's Quixote, Patti Smith anecdote and punk-era deaths
segments.summary: Al's Quixote, the connected restaurant, is described; Patti Smith recalled musicians there in 1969 before Woodstock. Patti Smith encouraged Dylan to perform Isis without guitar. The hosts then discuss Nancy Spungen's 1978 death in room 100, with Sid Vicious suspected but never tried, and Rufus Wainwright and Ethan Hawke's time there.

segments.title: Deaths, falls, and the 2011 sale and renovation
segments.summary: Earlier suicides and falls from windows are described. After the Bards' management, the building sold around 2011 for about eighty million dollars, staff were fired, art was removed, and the renovation became controversial. About forty original residents remain, with rent control. The documentary Dreaming Walls is recommended.

segments.title: Auctioned relics and closing discussion
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the auction of original doors and the iconic sign after its renovation, which included replacing letters that were sold off, and close the topic.

segments.title: Listener mail on finger spelling
segments.summary: A listener writes that they spell words in the sign language alphabet when stressed, and the hosts discuss listeners who trace or air-type words as a shared quirk.
